entry: Athenian statesman and general of the Golden Age of Athens. He was prominent and influential in Athenian politics between the [[Greco-Persian Wars]] and the [[Peloponnesian War]], and the historian [[Thucydides]], a contemporary, called him "the first citizen of Athens." Pericles turned the [[Delian League]] into an Athenian empire and led his countrymen during the first two years of the Peloponnesian War. He led Athens roughly from 461 to 429 BC, a period sometimes called the "Age of Pericles." He promoted the arts and literature, and the building project he started produced most of the surviving structures on the Acropolis, including the [[Parthenon]]. He fostered Athenian democracy so extensively that critics called him a populist. He died in the Plague of Athens in 429 BC, which weakened the city during its protracted conflict with [[Sparta]].

Yellow-green gem-quality variety of [[Olivine|olivine]], sometimes called chrysolite. Its magnesium-rich end member is called forsterite. Peridot is one of the few gemstones that occur in only one color, and its tint depends on iron content. It is found in lava, in mantle rock, in [[Basalt|volcanic basalt]] and in some meteorites. Along with [[Diamond|diamonds]], it is one of two gems known to form not in Earth's crust but in the molten rock of the upper mantle. Gem-quality peridot is rare at the surface because it is prone to alteration during its journey from deep within the mantle.

Part of the nervous system outside the brain and spinal cord, made of nerves and ganglia. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is one of two components of the nervous system of bilateral animals, the other being the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] (CNS). Its main function is to connect the CNS to the limbs and organs, relaying signals between the brain and spinal cord and the rest of the body. Unlike the CNS, it is not protected by the skull and vertebral column or by the blood-brain barrier, leaving it more vulnerable to injury. The PNS has somatic and autonomic divisions, each with sensory and motor sectors. The somatic division is under voluntary control, and humans have 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The autonomic division exerts involuntary control over smooth muscle and glands, such as those governing heart rate and [[Digestion|digestion]].

Order of odd-toed hoofed mammals, including [[Horse|horses]], [[Rhinoceros|rhinoceroses]] and [[Tapir|tapirs]]. The name comes from Greek words meaning "odd" and "finger, toe." About 17 living species belong to three families: Equidae (horses, asses and zebras), Rhinocerotidae (rhinoceroses), and Tapiridae (tapirs). The main axis of each foot passes through the third toe, the largest, and the other toes are reduced to varying degrees. Perissodactyls digest plant [[Cellulose|cellulose]] in their intestines, unlike most even-toed artiodactyls, which use stomach chambers. The order was far more diverse in the past, including the paraceratheres, which contained the largest known land mammals. The zoologist Richard Owen recognized in the 19th century that its families were related and coined the order's name.

Soil or underwater sediment frozen for at least two consecutive years. The oldest permafrost has remained frozen for around 700,000 years. About 15% of the exposed land surface of the Northern Hemisphere, and 11% of global land, is underlain by permafrost, around 18 million sq km in total, including large areas of [[Alaska]], Canada, Greenland and [[Siberia]]. It also occurs in high mountains such as the [[Tibetan Plateau]]. Permafrost holds large amounts of undecayed dead biomass, making tundra soil a [[Carbon|carbon]] sink. As it thaws, decomposition releases [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] or [[Methane|methane]], a feedback to [[Climate change|climate change]]. Estimates suggest nearly 70% of infrastructure built on permafrost is at risk by 2050, and 13,000 to 20,000 sites contaminated with toxic waste lie within it. A scientific review describes the risk of pathogens surviving the thaw as "generally low."

Mass extinction at the boundary of the [[Permian]] and [[Triassic]] periods, about 251.902 million years ago. It is Earth's most severe known extinction event, with 57% of biological families, 62% of genera, 81% of marine species and 70% of terrestrial vertebrate species lost. It is also the greatest known mass extinction of insects, and is called the Great Dying. The scientific consensus is that the main cause was the flood basalt eruptions that formed the [[Siberian Traps]], which released sulfur dioxide and [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. The result was euxinia (oxygen-starved, sulfurous oceans), elevated temperatures and acidified oceans. Atmospheric carbon dioxide rose from around 400 ppm to 2,500 ppm. Other proposed factors include [[Methane|methane]] released from methane clathrates and an extraterrestrial impact, though the chronology and mechanisms remain debated.

Geologic period and last division of the Paleozoic Era, spanning 47 million years. It ran from the end of the [[Carboniferous]] Period, 298.9 million years ago, to the beginning of the [[Triassic|Triassic]] Period, 251.902 million years ago. Sir Roderick Murchison introduced the name in 1841, after the Russian region of Perm. The period saw the diversification of synapsids and sauropsids (reptiles). The world was dominated by the supercontinent [[Pangaea]]. Desert expanded in continental interiors, and amniotes, better suited to drier conditions, rose to dominance over amphibians. At least three and possibly four major extinctions occurred, including the Capitanian mass extinction, associated with the Emeishan Traps. The period ended with the [[Permian–Triassic extinction event]], the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, associated with the Siberian Traps. On land, ecosystems took about 30 million years to recover.

Bijective function of a finite set onto itself, or a rearrangement of its members. When the set is ordered, a permutation changes the place of each member; the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} are the six arrangements of those numbers. The number of permutations of n distinct objects is n [[Factorial|factorial]] (n!), the product of the first n positive integers. The [[Function composition|composition]] of two permutations is a permutation, and all permutations of a set form a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] under this operation, the symmetric group of the set. The study of permutations is a starting point of [[Combinatorics|combinatorics]]. In computer science, a [[Sorting algorithm|sorting algorithm]] computes a permutation that puts data in natural order. Permutation-like hexagrams appeared in the *I Ching* in China. In 1677, Fabian Stedman described factorials when explaining the number of permutations of bells in change ringing.

State of northeastern [[Brazil|Brazil]], on the Atlantic coast (pop., 2024: 9.5 million). Its capital and largest city is [[Recife]], an important economic hub. The state inherits its name from the Captaincy of Pernambuco, established in 1534. European colonization began in the 16th century under mostly Portuguese rule, briefly interrupted by Dutch rule. Large numbers of enslaved Africans were brought to cultivate [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]], and much of the population has African ancestry. The state is known for [[Carnival|Carnival]] in Recife and in the colonial city of Olinda.

Human rights abuses against [[Uyghurs|Uyghurs]] and other Turkic Muslim minorities in [[Xinjiang|Xinjiang]], China, since 2014. Since 2017, an estimated one million people were held without legal process in camps officially called vocational education and training centers, the largest mass internment of an ethnic-religious minority since [[World War II|World War II]]. Reports also describe torture, mass surveillance, forced labor and forced sterilization. The U.S. Department of State declared the actions genocide in 2021; China denies committing abuses. In 2022, the UN human rights office said they may constitute crimes against humanity but did not use the term genocide.

Ceremonial capital of the [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Empire]], in the plains of Marvdasht, Fars province, [[Iran|Iran]]. Encircled by the southern [[Zagros Mountains|Zagros Mountains]], it is a [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] World Heritage Site. Its earliest remains date to 515 BC. The complex, raised on a walled platform, included five halls and grand entrances, and was occupied seasonally rather than as a city. Its exact function remains unclear. Most archaeologists long held that it was used for celebrating [[Nowruz|Nowruz]], the Persian New Year, and Iranian nobility and tributary peoples came to present gifts to the king, as shown in the stairway reliefs. In 330 BC the army of [[Alexander the Great|Alexander the Great]] took the complex, and its wooden parts were destroyed by fire. Exploration from the early 17th century led to the rediscovery of [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] writing.

Hero of [[Greek mythology|Greek mythology]] and legendary founder of the Perseid dynasty. Son of [[Zeus|Zeus]] and the mortal Danae, Perseus was, with Cadmus and Bellerophon, the greatest Greek hero and slayer of monsters before [[Heracles|Heracles]]; he was also Heracles's half-brother and great-grandfather. He beheaded the Gorgon [[Medusa|Medusa]] for King Polydectes and later rescued Andromeda from the sea monster Cetus. He accidentally killed his grandfather Acrisius with a quoit, fulfilling a prophecy. Perseus then founded and fortified Mycenae.

Uprising in [[Iran|Qajar Iran]] against absolute monarchy, 1905–1911. Driven by merchants, intellectuals and parts of the Shia clergy, it led to a 1906 constitution and a parliament, the Majlis. Protests in 1905 targeted a foreign customs director enforcing tariffs that repaid a loan financing the shah's European tour. Mohammad Ali Shah abolished the constitution and bombarded the parliament in 1908 with Russian and British support. Constitutionalist forces marched on Tehran, forced his abdication in favor of his young son, and reestablished the constitution in 1909. The revolution ended in December 1911 when the Second Majlis deputies were expelled with the support of 12,000 Russian troops. The constitution, though not adhered to, remained until the Islamic Revolution.

Inland sea of West Asia, between [[Iran|Iran]] and the [[Arabian Peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], sometimes called the Arabian Gulf. It is an extension of the [[Arabian Sea|Arabian Sea]] and the [[Indian Ocean|Indian Ocean]], connected to the Gulf of Oman by the [[Strait of Hormuz|Strait of Hormuz]]. It covers some 251,000 sq km and is about 989 km long, with a maximum depth of 90 m and an average of 50 m. The Shatt al-Arab delta forms its northwestern shore. The gulf has rich fishing grounds, reefs and pearl oysters, but its ecology has been damaged by industrialization and oil spills. Its basin began flooding about 15,000 years ago as sea levels rose. Its littoral states hold a large share of the world's oil and gas, and about 20 million barrels of petroleum liquids normally pass through the strait each day.

Visual arts of Persia (Iran) up to 1925, when the Qajar dynasty ended. Persian art has one of the richest heritages in world history, strong in architecture, painting, weaving, pottery, [[Calligraphy|calligraphy]], metalworking and sculpture. Rock art in Iran is its most ancient surviving art. From the [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Empire]] (550–330 BC), a large Iranian-speaking state ruled areas similar to modern Iran. Ancient monuments focus on the human figure, mostly male and often royal, and on animals. Under the [[Safavid dynasty|Safavid dynasty]] in the 16th century, a style combining plant motifs with Chinese cloud-bands spread across media from court artists. Painted pottery from [[Susa|Susa]] has been dated to around 5000 BC.

Long-haired breed of cat with a round face and petite muzzle. The first Persians may have been brought to Italy from [[Khorasan|Khorasan]] as early as 1620, and longhaired cats exported from [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan]] and [[Iran|Iran]] are documented from the 19th century. Selective breeding produced a wide range of coat colors and increasingly flat faces, which can cause breathing difficulties. Hereditary polycystic kidney disease affects almost half the population in some countries. In 2021 the Persian ranked as the fourth-most popular breed according to the Cat Fanciers' Association.

Western Iranian language, also known as Farsi, of the Indo-European family. It is official in [[Iran|Iran]], [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan]] and [[Tajikistan|Tajikistan]], where its three standard varieties are called Persian, Dari and Tajik. Approximately 130 million people speak it. Modern Persian continues Middle Persian, official language of the [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian Empire]], which descended from Old Persian of the [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Empire]], attested in cuneiform inscriptions from between the 6th and 4th century BCE. Persian was the first language to break the monopoly of Arabic on writing in the Muslim world. It was used as a language of bureaucracy by the Ottomans, the Delhi Sultanates, the Mughals and the Pashtuns. Modern Persian is written in the Perso-Arabic script, while Tajik uses a Cyrillic-based alphabet.

Body of written texts in the Persian language, spanning over two and a half millennia. Its sources lie in regions where Persian was native or official, including Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan, and some works were written by non-Persians. The bulk of surviving literature comes from after the [[Muslim conquest of Persia|Muslim conquest of Persia]], c. 650 CE. From the 9th to 11th centuries, a revival led by the Samanid, Saffarid and Ghaznavid dynasties developed New Persian literature, largely outside modern Iran. Poetry predominates, including the [[Ghazal|ghazal]]. Major works include the *Shahnameh* of [[Ferdowsi|Ferdowsi]], completed around 1010 CE, which preserved Iranian myths and history; the works of [[Rumi|Rumi]]; the *Rubaiyat* of [[Omar Khayyam|Omar Khayyam]]; and the poetry of [[Hafez|Hafez]].

Myths told by the ancient Persians and other Iranian peoples, concerning the origin of the world, deities, heroes and monsters. The myths reflect a battle between good and evil. In Zoroastrian dualism, the creator [[Ahura Mazda|Ahura Mazda]] opposes the destructive Ahriman and his demonic Divs. The only written religious texts come from the prophet [[Zoroaster|Zoroaster]], whose reforms became [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]]. Heroes include Kaveh, who led a popular uprising against the tyrant Zahhak, and the warrior Rostam in [[Ferdowsi|Ferdowsi's]] *Shahnameh*. Birds such as the Simurgh were usually omens of good, while snakes symbolized evil. Scholars must reconstruct the myths from fragmentary and disparate sources.

Edible fruit of trees in the genus [[Diospyros|Diospyros]]. The most widely cultivated is the Chinese, Korean and Japanese kaki persimmon, *Diospyros kaki*, native to China and Northeast India. Botanically a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], its ripe fruit is high in sugars, mainly [[Sucrose|sucrose]], fructose and glucose. The flesh is astringent until fully ripe. China produced 80% of the world's persimmons in 2023. *Diospyros kaki* was first cultivated in China more than 2,000 years ago and introduced to Japan in the 7th century.

Computer designed to be operated directly by an individual end user rather than an expert or technician. Typical tasks include word processing, web browsing, email, spreadsheets, gaming and video calling. Unlike minicomputers and mainframes, personal computers are not time-shared. Advances in semiconductor technology, such as the silicon [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]], made them possible. In 1981 the [[IBM|IBM]] Personal Computer was released, and IBM PC compatibles soon followed; the term PC came to refer mainly to them. Since the early 1990s, machines running [[Microsoft|Microsoft]] Windows on [[Intel|Intel]] x86 processors dominated the market. Alternatives such as [[MacOS|macOS]] on Apple's Mac platform and Linux-based systems hold a minority share. The Apple II, TRS-80 and Commodore 64 were called home computers.

Protective [[Clothing|clothing]], [[Helmet|helmets]], goggles and other gear designed to protect the wearer from injury or infection. Hazards include physical, electrical, heat, chemical, biological and airborne particulate matter. PPE is worn for [[Occupational safety and health|occupational]] safety and for [[Sport|sports]] and recreation. It is needed when hazards are present and engineering and administrative controls cannot reduce risks to acceptable levels. PPE does not eliminate the hazard at its source, and workers are exposed if the equipment fails. Each item is a barrier that can cause strain and discomfort, so good ergonomic design matters. In the hierarchy of hazard controls, PPE ranks last. Sixteenth-century plague doctors wore protective uniforms, and scientific PPE is generally traced to cloth facemasks promoted by Wu Lien-teh during the 1910–11 Manchurian [[Plague (disease)|pneumonic plague]] outbreak.

Mental disorder characterized by an enduring, pervasive pattern of maladaptive behavior, emotions, cognition and inner experience that deviates from social norms. The pattern develops early, is inflexible and causes significant distress or impairment, especially in interpersonal relationships. The [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization]] ICD-11 classifies personality disorders dimensionally, by severity and traits, while the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM-5-TR) uses categories. Categorical models have been criticized for weak evidence, heavy comorbidity and stigma. Among psychiatric patients, prevalence is estimated between 40 and 60%. Treatment is primarily [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapeutic]], including dialectical behavior therapy for [[Borderline personality disorder|borderline personality disorder]]. Some experts contest the validity of diagnoses, arguing that they reflect social and cultural judgments.

[[Psychology|Branch of psychology]] that examines personality and how it varies among individuals. Its areas of focus include describing what personality is, documenting how it develops, explaining the mental processes behind it, and providing a framework for understanding individuals. The word personality comes from the [[Latin|Latin]] *persona*, meaning "mask." In 1937 [[Gordon Allport|Gordon Allport]] distinguished nomothetic psychology, which seeks general laws such as the traits of [[Extraversion and introversion|extraversion and introversion]], from idiographic psychology, which studies the unique individual. Major traditions include trait, psychodynamic, humanistic, biological, behaviorist, evolutionary and social learning perspectives. Many researchers take an eclectic approach. Debates include [[Free will|free will]] versus determinism and heredity versus environment.

Anthropomorphic figures of death found in many religions and mythologies. In modern stories the Grim Reaper, usually a robed [[Skeleton|skeleton]] with a scythe, collects the soul of the dying. Other beliefs hold that death is a benevolent psychopomp that guides the soul to the [[Afterlife|afterlife]] without controlling when or how a person dies. Death is most often male, but it is female in some cultures, such as Santa Muerte in [[Mexico|Mexico]]. Spanish speakers personify death as female, and the Aztec goddess Mictecacihuatl, "Queen of Mictlan," ruled the underworld. Death is also one of the [[Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse|Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse]]. San La Muerte, a skeletal folk saint, is venerated in [[Paraguay|Paraguay]] and northeast Argentina.
